identification.name: Kevlar 49 / Epoxy (Unidirectional, 0°)
identification.common_form_notes: Supplied as unidirectional prepreg tape (Solvay CYCOM 985 resin system, 177°C/350°F autoclave cure) and laid up into panels/plates, matching the unidirectional carbon fibre entry in this database's construction method (0° fibre orientation, not woven fabric).
identification.notes: Values are for the 0° (fibre-direction) properties of a unidirectional Kevlar 49/epoxy laminate — directly comparable in architecture to the unidirectional carbon fibre/epoxy entry in this database (same 0° layup convention), giving a clean fibre-type comparison (aramid vs. carbon) at similar construction. DATA GAP: this source (a MatWeb datasheet transcribed from an aerospace qualification test program) reports tensile modulus, compressive strength/modulus, and interlaminar shear strength at multiple temperatures and moisture conditions, but does NOT report tensile strength, Poisson's ratio, or any thermal properties (CTE, thermal conductivity, specific heat) at all — checked the raw source directly and via two supplementary searches (the actual manufacturer TDS PDF exists but sits behind active Cloudflare bot-protection, so wasn't fetched). Left tensile_strength null rather than substitute a compressive or modulus figure; this is a genuine limitation of this specific source, not a reflection of the material — Kevlar 49's whole reputation is built on exceptional tensile strength-to-weight (~3000+ MPa for the fibre itself), so a future source with that number would meaningfully improve this entry. A real, well-known characteristic of aramid composites IS captured here: compressive strength (214 MPa dry) is dramatically lower than the modulus values would suggest for a material this stiff — aramid fibres buckle/kink under compressive load far more readily than carbon or glass fibres, giving Kevlar composites a pronounced tension/compression strength asymmetry (their key design weakness) — this is the composite-fibre analog to the crystal-structure-driven tension/compression asymmetry already noted on the Magnesium AZ31B entry, though the underlying mechanism (fibre microbuckling vs. crystallographic twinning) is completely different. Also moisture-sensitive: compressive strength drops from 214 MPa dry to 165 MPa wet, and shear strength from 37.2 MPa dry to 34.5 MPa wet at room temperature — smaller effect than Nylon 6's moisture sensitivity elsewhere in this database, but real. Shear strength (37.2 MPa) is specifically interlaminar (short-beam/ILSS test method) — a matrix-dominated through-thickness property, not in-plane fibre-direction shear; not derived via von Mises, since that criterion doesn't apply to anisotropic fibre composites the way it does to isotropic ductile metals. All values are room-temperature (24°C), dry condition, 0° fibre direction unless otherwise noted.

typical_usage: Impact-resistant and ballistic-protection panels, and applications where toughness/damage tolerance matters more than raw stiffness or compressive strength: helmets, vehicle armor panels, and protective enclosures. Compared to the carbon fibre/epoxy entry in this database: choose Kevlar for better impact toughness and damage tolerance; choose carbon fibre instead for higher stiffness and much better compressive strength, since Kevlar's fibre-buckling weakness in compression is a serious design constraint for load-bearing structural members.
